Network Topology Types - Shapes and What They Mean
1. Point-to-point
One dedicated link between two nodes.
Full-duplex Ethernet has no contention.
2. Bus
Every node taps the same backbone cable.
Cheap, but one shared medium for all
traffic.
3. Ring
Each node links to two neighbours in a
closed loop; data circulates around it.
4. Star
Every node has its own link to one central
device (hub or switch).
5. Tree / extended star
Stars cascaded under a root device - a
hierarchy of central devices.
6. Mesh
Nodes cross-linked with many redundant
paths - full or partial mesh.
7. Hybrid
Any mix of the above; typical of large real-
world networks.
Read the shape, not the name: how nodes connect decides whether they share one medium (bus, hub star) or get their own link (point-to-point, switched
star).

Which Topologies Apply to Ethernet - and Why
Topology
Used in Ethernet?
Clarification / justification
Point
-to-point
Yes
- the norm today
Switched full
-duplex links are point-to-point. Automotive 100BASE-T1 and 1000BASE-T1 also use point-to
-
point links.
Bus
Legacy and modern
Historical bus Ethernet means legacy 10BASE5/10BASE2 coax. Modern 10BASE
-T1S supports a shared
multidrop medium.
Star (hub)
Historical only
10/100BASE
-T with a hub: star wiring, but still one collision domain. Explains why switching was needed.
Star (switch)
Yes
- standard LAN
Each device has a separate switch link. Full
-duplex operation removes collisions on that link.
Extended star / tree
Yes
- for scale
Switches cascaded in layers. Same switched
behaviour, just more ports and distance.
Ring
Yes
- with redundancy
Ethernet can use physical rings with RSTP, MRP or HSR. PRP instead uses two independent parallel LANs.
Mesh
Yes
- redundant paths
Redundant Layer
-
2 paths need loop prevention or a suitable forwarding architecture. Spanning tree is one
solution.
Hybrid
Implicitly
Any large network mixes the above, but it adds no new Ethernet
behaviour to learn.
Why the module shows only four: bus, hub star, switched star and extended star introduce shared media and switching. Ethernet can also use rings and
meshes with suitable redundancy control. Automotive 10BASE-T1S adds a modern multidrop example.
Hub, Switch and Router - Who Looks at What
Layer 1
HUB
Looks at: nothing - no addresses at all
Action: repeats every incoming signal out of all other ports
Layer 2
SWITCH
Looks at: destination MAC address
Known unicast: forwards to the learned port
Multicast: may forward to multiple ports
Layer 3
ROUTER
Looks at: destination IP address
Action: forwards the packet towards another IP network
Where each device sits in a network
PC A
PC B
Printer
SWITCH ROUTER
Other IP
network
Same network
forwards by MAC
Network boundary
forwards by IP
Rule of thumb - which device does the job?
•Traffic stays inside one Layer-2 network -> the SWITCH decides, using MAC
addresses.
•Traffic must reach a different IP network -> the ROUTER decides, using IP
addresses.
•A HUB decides nothing - it copies signals everywhere, so all ports share one
collision domain.
the higher the layer, the more the device understands - a hub reads no address, a switch forwards frames by MAC, a router forwards packets by IP.
What Is a MAC Address?
Definition
A Media Access Control address is a data-link-layer address
associated with a network interface.
Example: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E
•Total length: 48 bits
•Shown as six hexadecimal octets
•Each hex digit is four bits; each pair is one byte
Address fields in a frame
Destination MAC ---> intended receiver or receiver group
Source MAC ---> transmitting interface
MAC address versus IP address
MAC address IP address
Local Layer-2 delivery Layer-3 addressing and routing
Examined by switches Examined by routers
In the Ethernet header In the IP header
Identifies an interface Identifies a network endpoint
A MAC address identifies a network interface, not an entire device. A
device with several interfaces has several MAC addresses.
MAC addresses support local frame delivery; IP addresses support communication across IP networks.
Address structure: MA-L uses a 24-bit OUI plus 24 assigned bits. MA-M, MA-S and local addresses differ. In the first octet, I/G (bit 0): individual (0) or group (1). U/L (bit 1): universally (0)
or locally (1) administered. Local addresses need not identify a manufacturer.
ARP: Finding the Next-Hop MAC Address for IPv4
Problem
For IPv4 over Ethernet, the frame needs the MAC address of the next
hop on the local link.
How ARP resolves it
•Select the next hop: local host or router/default gateway
•Check the ARP cache for that next-hop IPv4 address
•If absent, broadcast a request to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
•Normally, the target replies by unicast (no proxy ARP)
•Cache the next-hop IPv4-to-MAC mapping
•Send the frame to that MAC, keeping the final IP destination
Request and reply at a glance
Field ARP request / reply
EtherType
0x0806 in both directions
Destination MAC (request)
FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
- broadcast
Destination MAC (reply)
The requester's MAC
- unicast
Carried in
The Ethernet payload, not inside
an IP packet
Result
A next
-hop IPv4-to-
MAC mapping
in the ARP cache
Who has 192.168.1.20? -> 192.168.1.20 is at 00:AA:BB:CC:DD:EE
On-link destination: resolve the host MAC. Off-link destination: resolve the router MAC.
IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery rather than ARP.

Learn from the SOURCE address - forward using the DESTINATION address.
What the switch does, in order
1The frame arrives on Port 1.
2It reads the SOURCE address, MAC-A.
3It records: MAC-A is reachable via Port 1.
4It looks up the DESTINATION, MAC-B.
5MAC-B is not in the table yet - destination unknown.
6So it floods the frame out of all other eligible ports in the same VLAN.
Forwarding table after this frame
Before this frame the table was completely empty.
source-address learning builds the forwarding table automatically - an unknown destination is simply flooded until the switch has learned where it lives.

The switch learns source MAC addresses from incoming frames.
What the switch does, in order
1The reply arrives on Port 2.
2It learns: MAC-B is reachable via Port 2.
3It looks up the destination, MAC-A - already in the table.
4It forwards the frame through Port 1 only. No flooding.

Learned MAC Port
MAC-A Port 1
MAC-B Port 2
BEFORE - destination unknown
flood out of all other ports
AFTER - destination known
forward through one port only
once both addresses are learned, known-unicast frames are forwarded through the single required port - which is why a switched network does not waste
bandwidth the way a hub does.
Ethernet Switch Forwarding Decisions
Case 1: Known unicast
Destination MAC is in the table
Forward through that port
Case 2: Unknown unicast
Destination MAC is not in table
Flood other eligible ports in the same VLAN
Case 3: Broadcast
Destination FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
Flood within the VLAN broadcast domain
Case 4: Multicast
Unregistered multicast is commonly flooded within the VLAN.
IGMP snooping limits IPv4 multicast, MLD snooping limits IPv6.
Static filters, switch policy and reserved-address rules also apply.
Case 5: Same incoming port
Destination maps to the port the frame arrived on
Do not send it back out through that port
Forwarding depends on the destination MAC, VLAN, forwarding
table, port state and filtering policy.
Table aging: a learned entry is deleted if no frame is seen from that MAC for the
aging time (commonly 300 s). The address must then be learned again, and traffic to
it is flooded in the meantime.

Key takeaway: every frame does two jobs at once - it teaches the switch where its sender lives (MAC-C on Port 3) and is then delivered only to the port of
its destination (Port 2).
Loops, Broadcast Storms and Spanning Tree
The problem: a Layer-2 loop
Two switches joined by two parallel links
A broadcast or unknown unicast is flooded to all other ports
What happens next
The flooded frame returns over the second link
It is flooded again - endlessly, in both directions
Three symptoms
Broadcast storm, unstable MAC tables, duplicate frames
An Ethernet frame has no TTL, so nothing stops it
The solution: spanning tree
Switches exchange BPDUs
They form a loop-free active tree.
Redundant ports block traffic until needed.
If an active link fails
A blocked link is brought back into forwarding
Redundancy without a permanent loop
Ethernet has no hop limit, so a Layer-2 loop is fatal. Spanning tree
blocks redundant links until they are needed.
Standards: STP (IEEE 802.1D), RSTP (802.1w) and MSTP. The PDF examples show
faster MRP recovery than RSTP. Actual recovery depends on the
implementation.
Knowledge Check 3
Question 1
A switch receives a frame on Port 4. Which address does it use for
learning?
•A. Destination IP address
•B. Source IP address
•C. Destination MAC address
•D. Source MAC address
Question 2
Which address does a switch examine when selecting an output
port?
•A. Source MAC address
•B. Destination MAC address
•C. UDP source port
•D. Application name
Question 3
What does a switch do with an unknown-unicast frame?
•A. Always discard it
•B. Send it to a router only
•C. Flood it through other eligible ports in the same VLAN
•D. Replace its destination address
Question 4
What is the Ethernet broadcast MAC address?
•A. 00:00:00:00:00:00
•B. FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
•C. 11:11:11:11:11:11
•D. AA:AA:AA:AA:AA:AA
Answers
1. D 2. B 3. C 4. B
Why these answers
Learn from the SOURCE MAC; forward using the DESTINATION MAC
Unknown destination = flood in the VLAN; FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF = broadcast
